title: Technical accuracy: sentences, punctuation and spelling
specPoints: AO6 on both papers: 16 marks for technical accuracy on each Question 5, a fifth of the qualification

tips.title: A fifth of the GCSE, marked apart
tips.body: Sixteen marks on each writing question, thirty-two in all, on a scale that the content mark cannot rescue. It is the most controllable fifth of the exam, because the errors are the same every year.

tips.title: The check, in order
tips.body: Ends of sentences; speech; apostrophes; the five hardest words letter by letter; the ending. Five minutes, every time, on both papers. Read the piece backwards if the errors hide.

tips.title: The comma that holds two sentences
tips.body: If what is on each side of a comma could stand as a sentence, the comma is a splice. A full stop, a semicolon or a joining word; never a comma alone.

tips.title: It's is it is
tips.body: It's, who's, they're: apostrophe means letters left out. Its, whose, their: no apostrophe, possessive. Say the long form aloud; if it does not fit, drop the apostrophe.

tips.title: A plain word beats a misspelt ambitious one
tips.body: A wrong ambitious word costs on the spelling bullet and earns nothing on the vocabulary bullet. If the doubled consonant will not come, use the word you can spell.

tips.title: For effect is the phrase
tips.body: A range of sentence forms is credited when each is placed to do something: the short one at the turn, the long one where the mind runs. A checklist of forms earns nothing.

why.matters: Punctuation is not decoration on writing; it is part of the grammar, and a comma in the wrong place changes what a sentence says. The exam gives a fifth of the whole qualification to accuracy because a piece of writing that cannot be relied on to say what it means fails at its first job, however good its ideas. The marks are also the most controllable in the paper: the errors are the same every year, and five minutes with a finger on every full stop moves the accuracy level in a way no idea can. The habit lasts beyond the exam, because every email, form and message is read by someone who notices.

examples.title: The message that was read the wrong way
examples.body: A text sent without the comma, an email whose sentences run into each other, a notice with an apostrophe in the plural: each is read by someone, and each says something slightly other than what was meant, or says that the writer did not care. The five-minute check the exam trains is the check that every piece of writing sent to another person deserves, and the people who make that check without thinking are the ones whose writing is trusted.

examples.title: The form, the reference, the covering letter
examples.body: Any writing that decides something, a job form, a complaint, a reference, a statement, is read first for whether it can be relied on, and accuracy is the first thing a reader sees. The reader who notices would of, or the missing full stop, has stopped attending to the argument. AO6 is the exam's name for the fact that accuracy is the price of being listened to.

steps.title: Sixteen marks on each paper, a fifth of the GCSE
steps.body:
AO6 is *use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures for clarity, purpose and effect, with accurate spelling and punctuation*, and the mark scheme adds that it must be twenty per cent of the marks for the whole qualification. Sixteen marks on Paper 1 Question 5, sixteen on Paper 2 Question 5: thirty-two of the hundred and sixty.

**Four levels.** Level 4, 13 to 16: sentence demarcation consistently secure and accurate; a wide range of punctuation used with a high level of accuracy; a full range of sentence forms for effect; Standard English consistently and appropriately, with secure control of complex grammatical structures; a high level of accuracy in spelling, including ambitious vocabulary; extensive and ambitious vocabulary. Level 3, 9 to 12: mostly secure; a range of punctuation mostly successful; a variety of sentence forms; mostly Standard English; generally accurate spelling including complex words. Level 2, 5 to 8: demarcation mostly secure and sometimes accurate; some control of punctuation; attempts at variety. Level 1, 1 to 4: occasional demarcation; some conscious punctuation; simple forms.

**Marked separately from content.** A compelling piece with four comma splices sits at Level 4 for AO5 and Level 3 or lower for AO6. The two scales never rescue each other, and the second is decided in the five minutes a writer keeps to check.

rows: Demarcation consistently secure; wide range of punctuation, accurate; full range of forms for effect
Mostly secure; a range of punctuation, mostly successful; a variety of forms
Mostly secure, sometimes accurate; some control; variety attempted
Occasional demarcation; some conscious punctuation; simple forms

steps.title: Sentence demarcation: the first bullet
steps.body:
Demarcation means marking where a sentence starts and stops: a capital at one end, a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark at the other. It is the first bullet at every level because it is the error examiners see most.

**The comma splice.** Two sentences joined with a comma: *The street was empty, nothing moved.* Either a full stop, *The street was empty. Nothing moved.*, or a joining word, *The street was empty and nothing moved*, or a semicolon, *The street was empty; nothing moved.* A comma alone cannot hold two sentences together.

**The run-on.** Sentences joined by *and* or *then* until the paragraph is one sentence long. Cut at the point where the reader would breathe.

**The fragment.** A group of words with no main clause, so it cannot stand on its own: *Which was how I knew.* Chosen, after a full sentence, it is a sentence form for effect. Unchosen, three times a paragraph, it is a demarcation error. The difference is whether the writer could say why it is there.

**The check.** Read the piece with a finger on every full stop and ask whether what is between this one and the last is one sentence.

rows: The street was empty, nothing moved.
The street was empty. Nothing moved.
He looked at the box and then at me and then he sat down and then he sighed
He looked at the box, then at me. He sat down. He sighed.
Because she had already decided. And made the tea. And waited.
She had already decided, made the tea and waited.
She had made the tea before I got there. Which was the first sign.
Kept: a form used for effect after a full sentence

visuals.alt: A table of demarcation errors, the comma splice, the run-on and the unchosen fragment, with a corrected version of each, and a chosen fragment kept

check.prompt: Which of these is a comma splice?
check.solution: Two complete sentences joined by a comma alone is a comma splice. A comma with *and*, a semicolon, or a subordinate clause with *although* are all correct ways of joining the same two ideas.

markScheme.description: The street was empty, nothing moved

options: Although the street was empty, nothing moved
The street was empty, and nothing moved
The street was empty, nothing moved
The street was empty; nothing moved

steps.title: A wide range of punctuation, used with a high level of accuracy
steps.body:
The Level 4 descriptor wants range and accuracy together. Five marks beyond the full stop and the comma, each with one job.

**The semicolon** joins two sentences that belong together: *She had decided; she let me argue anyway.* Both halves could stand alone.

**The colon** introduces: a list, an explanation, a reveal. *There was one thing on the dresser: a box of keys.*

**The dash** interrupts or adds an afterthought, and a pair of dashes brackets an aside: *The tea—already made—was the first sign.* Mansfield's self-correcting sentence, “something light and sad—no, not sad, exactly—something gentle”, is a pair of dashes showing a mind change course.

**Brackets** hold something the sentence could do without. **The ellipsis** trails off, and is used once.

**Speech marks.** A new line for each new speaker; the punctuation of the speech inside the closing mark; a comma, not a full stop, before *she said* when the sentence continues: *"Sit down," she said, "and tell me again."*

**Apostrophes.** Possession, *my grandmother's house*; omission, *it's* for it is; never for a plural. *Its* without an apostrophe is the possessive.

check.prompt: Which sentence uses the colon correctly?
check.solution: A colon introduces what follows from a complete statement: the thing on the dresser, then what it was. Placed after *was* or after *thing* it breaks the sentence where nothing is being introduced.

steps.title: A full range of sentence forms for effect
steps.body:
The descriptor says *for effect*: the forms are varied on purpose, and the purpose is visible. Four forms cover most of the range.

**The simple sentence.** One clause. *Nothing moved.* Placed after a long sentence, it stops the reader.

**The compound sentence.** Two clauses joined by *and*, *but*, *or*, *so*. It moves the reader along, and it is the form to cut when a paragraph runs on.

**The complex sentence.** A main clause with a subordinate one: *Although she had made the tea, she let me argue.* The subordinate clause can go first, last, or in the middle, and moving it changes the emphasis.

**The forms that are also voices.** The exclamation, “Little rogue!”; the question a narrator asks themselves; the list that piles up; the one-word sentence.

**How the examiner sees it.** Not by counting forms, but by noticing that the short sentence sits where the turn is, that the long one runs where the character's mind runs, that a question opens a paragraph and the paragraph answers it.

rows: The street was empty and the dog lay where it had stopped.
Although she had made the tea, she let me argue.
props.title: Forms, for effect

visuals.alt: A table of five sentence forms with an example and the effect of each: simple, compound, complex, exclamation and one word

check.prompt: What does the descriptor mean by a full range of sentence forms for effect?
check.solution: For effect is the phrase that matters. A form is credited when it is placed to do something the reader can feel. A checklist of forms, or one form used throughout, is not a range for effect.

markScheme.description: Forms varied on purpose, with the purpose visible: the short sentence at the turn, the long one where the mind runs, the question the paragraph answers

options: Forms varied on purpose, with the purpose visible: the short sentence at the turn, the long one where the mind runs, the question the paragraph answers
Short sentences throughout, because short sentences are easier to demarcate and so raise the accuracy mark
Every kind of sentence used at least once in the piece, ticked off a list of simple, compound, complex, question and exclamation, whether or not any of them does anything for the reader
Long sentences throughout, because long sentences show a wider vocabulary and more complex grammar than short ones

steps.title: Correcting a paragraph
steps.body: Here is a paragraph as a student might write it in the last five minutes, and the same paragraph after a check. Seven errors; the notes name each.

visuals.problem: Find and fix the seven errors in: She had made the tea before I got there, it was the first sign. "Sit down" she said "and tell me again why I should leave the house I was born in". I began at the begining, my grandmother did not make tea for people she intended to agree with, she made it for people who's arguments she had already won.

steps.text: Comma splice: *before I got there, it was the first sign* → *before I got there. It was the first sign.*
steps.note: Two sentences; a full stop, or a semicolon.

steps.text: Speech punctuation: *"Sit down" she said "and tell me again …"* → *"Sit down," she said, "and tell me again …"*
steps.note: A comma inside the closing mark, and a comma after *said* when the speech continues.

steps.text: The full stop belongs inside the closing speech mark: *… I was born in."*
steps.note: The punctuation of the speech goes inside.
A doubled consonant, the commonest class of spelling slip in ambitious words.

steps.text: Comma splice again: *at the beginning, my grandmother did not …* → *at the beginning. My grandmother did not …*
steps.note: The second splice hides behind a long sentence.

steps.text: Apostrophe: *who's arguments* → *whose arguments*; and the last comma joins two sentences too: *agree with; she made it* or a full stop.
steps.note: *Who's* is who is. The possessive is *whose*.

rows: it was the first sign, after a comma
A comma cannot hold two sentences
Comma inside the closing mark; comma after said
Whose is possessive; who's is who is

check.prompt: Why does the corrected paragraph keep some commas and replace others with full stops?
check.solution: The test for every comma is whether what is on each side of it could be a sentence on its own. If both could, the comma is a splice and a full stop or semicolon replaces it; if not, the comma is doing its proper job and stays.

markScheme.description: A comma stays where it separates parts of one sentence and goes where it was holding two sentences together, which it cannot do

options: Full stops are always better than commas in exam writing, so every comma should be replaced by a full stop wherever the sentence allows it, and the piece will read more clearly as a result
A comma stays where it separates parts of one sentence and goes where it was holding two sentences together, which it cannot do
Commas are only allowed in speech, so the ones outside the speech marks are replaced and the ones inside are kept
The examiners count commas and full stops and want equal numbers of each in every paragraph

steps.title: Standard English and control of complex grammar
steps.body:
The fourth bullet at Level 4 is Standard English used consistently and appropriately, with secure control of complex grammatical structures. Four places where control goes.

**Agreement.** *The box of keys were on the dresser* → *was*: the subject is the box. *Each of them have* → *has*.

**Tense.** A story that starts in the past and slips into the present for a paragraph has lost control; a story that shifts tense at the turn, on purpose, has used a form for effect. The difference, again, is whether the writer could say why.

**Pronouns.** *Me and my grandmother argued* → *My grandmother and I argued*; *between you and I* → *between you and me*.

**The forms that are not Standard English.** *Would of*, *should of* → *would have*, *should have*. *Them keys* → *those keys*. *I never did nothing* → *I never did anything*. Inside speech marks, dialect and non-standard forms are a choice and are credited as one; in the narration, they are errors.

**Complex structures, controlled.** A sentence with three clauses in the right order, a participle phrase attached to the right noun, a relative clause that follows what it describes: *The box, which she had packed herself, sat on the dresser.*

rows: The box of keys were on the dresser
The box of keys was on the dresser
The subject is the box, singular
Walking to the station, the rain started
Walking to the station, I felt the rain start
The participle must attach to the walker

check.prompt: Which sentence keeps Standard English in the narration while letting a character speak in dialect?
check.solution: Inside the speech marks a character may speak as she speaks; the narration outside them stays standard. Dialect in the narration, or a non-standard pronoun in the narrator's own sentence, is an error rather than a choice.

steps.title: Five sentences, five errors
steps.body:
Each sentence has one error. Name its class, then fix it.

1. The house was quiet, everyone had gone to bed.
2. "Where are you going" she asked.
3. Its been a long day and the dog wants it's dinner.
4. Each of the children were waiting by the gate.
5. She was definately going to say no.

Then read a paragraph of your own writing the same way: a finger on every full stop, a look at every apostrophe, and the five most ambitious words checked letter by letter.

boxes.title: Speech

boxes.title: Apostrophes

boxes.title: Ambitious words

visuals.alt: Four boxes giving the five-minute check: full stops, speech, apostrophes and the ambitious words

check.prompt: What is the error in: Its been a long day and the dog wants it's dinner?
check.solution: It's, with an apostrophe, is it is or it has; its, without one, is the possessive. The sentence has each where the other belongs. It is the commonest apostrophe error on the paper and the easiest to find in a check.

markScheme.description: The apostrophes are the wrong way round: it's been a long day, and the dog wants its dinner

options: There is a comma missing before and, which is needed in every compound sentence of this kind and is the only error in the sentence as written
The sentence is a run-on and should be split into two sentences at the word and
The word dinner should be capitalised, since it is the name of a meal
The apostrophes are the wrong way round: it's been a long day, and the dog wants its dinner

steps.title: Ambitious vocabulary, spelt: the check in order
steps.body:
The last two bullets at Level 4 are a high level of accuracy in spelling, including ambitious vocabulary, and extensive and ambitious use of vocabulary. Together they set a trap: the more ambitious the word, the likelier the slip, and a misspelt ambitious word costs on both bullets.

**The words that go wrong.** Doubled consonants, *beginning*, *occurred*, *necessary*; *-ly* on words ending in *e*, *definitely*, *completely*; *-ent* and *-ant*, *independent*, *relevant*; the silent letters, *rhythm*, *conscience*; the homophones, *their*, *there*, *they're*; *whose*, *who's*; *affect*, *effect*.

**The check, in order.** First the ends of sentences, because a splice costs the first bullet. Then the speech, because that is where a story's punctuation goes. Then every apostrophe. Then the five most ambitious words, letter by letter, and if one cannot be spelt, a plainer word that can. Then the ending, to make sure it is there.

**Reading backwards.** Reading the piece from the last sentence to the first breaks the flow that hides errors, because the eye stops predicting and starts seeing.

**And the register.** The vocabulary the top band wants is chosen for exactness, which is the AO5 lesson: *powdered* over *very bright*. Ambition is not length.

check.prompt: A student cannot remember whether a word is spelt with one consonant or two, and there are two minutes left. What is the best move?
check.solution: The spelling bullet says accuracy including ambitious vocabulary, and a wrong ambitious word is wrong twice. A plain word that is right is credited for accuracy and costs nothing on vocabulary that a single word would have earned.

markScheme.description: Replace it with a plainer word that is certainly right, because a misspelt ambitious word costs on two bullets and a plain word costs on none

options: Replace it with a plainer word that is certainly right, because a misspelt ambitious word costs on two bullets and a plain word costs on none
Leave it, because the examiners give credit for attempting ambitious vocabulary even when it is misspelt, and the vocabulary bullet outweighs the spelling bullet on the AO6 scale
Write both spellings, one after the other, so that the examiner can choose the correct one
Underline it, because underlined words are not counted for spelling accuracy

steps.title: Technical accuracy in one page
steps.body:
Thirty-two marks across the two papers, a fifth of the GCSE, decided in the five minutes a writer keeps at the end of each writing question.

- **Demarcation first:** a capital and a stop on every sentence; no comma splices; fragments only when chosen.
- **Punctuation with a job:** the semicolon joins, the colon introduces, the dash interrupts; speech on a new line with the punctuation inside; apostrophes for possession and omission, never plurals.
- **Sentence forms for effect:** the short one placed, the long one where the mind runs, the exclamation as a voice.
- **Standard English in the narration:** agreement, tense, pronouns, have not of; dialect only inside speech marks, as a choice.
- **Ambitious vocabulary, spelt:** doubled consonants, -ly, -ent and -ant, homophones; a plain word beats a misspelt ambitious one.
- **The check, in order:** ends of sentences, speech, apostrophes, the five hard words, the ending. Read backwards.

The two scales are marked apart. Content cannot rescue accuracy, and accuracy is the easier of the two to fix.

check.prompt: How many marks are given for technical accuracy across the two Language papers together?
check.solution: Thirty-two: sixteen on each Question 5. It is a fifth of the hundred and sixty marks in the qualification, which the scheme says AO6 must constitute, and it is the fifth most within a writer's control.

questions.prompt: How many marks for technical accuracy are there on one Question 5?
questions.solution: 16 marks on each paper's Question 5, on the AO6 scale, alongside 24 for content and organisation. Across the two papers that is 32 of the 160, a fifth of the GCSE.

questions.prompt: What is the correct version of: The street was empty, nothing moved.
questions.solution: Two sentences need a full stop or a semicolon between them, or a joining word. A comma alone is a splice, and adding more commas or removing the one there does not make one sentence of two.

markScheme.description: The street was empty. Nothing moved.

options: The street, was empty, nothing moved.
The street was empty, nothing, moved.
The street was empty nothing moved.
The street was empty. Nothing moved.

questions.prompt: Which word is misspelt in: She was definately going to say no?
questions.solution: Definitely: the -ly is added to definite, and the middle vowel is i, not a. It is among the most misspelt ambitious words on the paper, and the check catches it letter by letter.

markScheme.description: definately

questions.prompt: Which is the possessive form: the dog wants ___ dinner?
questions.solution: Its, with no apostrophe, is the possessive; it's is it is or it has. The rule runs against the usual one for possession, which is why it is the commonest apostrophe error in the exam.

markScheme.description: its

options: its
it is
it's
its'

questions.prompt: Which sentence punctuates the speech correctly?
questions.solution: The comma sits inside the closing mark after *down*, a comma follows *said* because the speech continues, and the full stop at the end is inside the final mark. Speech is where a story's punctuation is tested hardest.

markScheme.description: "Sit down," she said, "and tell me again."

options: "Sit down" she said "and tell me again".
"Sit down," she said, "and tell me again."
"Sit down." She said, "and tell me again."
"Sit down, she said, and tell me again."

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a chosen fragment and a demarcation error?
questions.solution: Which was the first sign, after a full sentence, is a form used for effect. Because she had already decided. And made the tea. And waited, is three fragments doing nothing. The examiner reads the difference as control.

markScheme.description: A chosen fragment follows a full sentence and does something the writer could name; an unchosen one lacks a main clause by accident

options: A chosen fragment is in speech and an unchosen one is in narration
There is no difference: a fragment is always an error, and every sentence must have a main clause of its own, whatever effect the writer had in mind
A chosen fragment follows a full sentence and does something the writer could name; an unchosen one lacks a main clause by accident
A chosen fragment is one word long and an unchosen one is longer

questions.prompt: Which sentence shows secure control of a complex grammatical structure?
questions.solution: A relative clause set off by commas, following the noun it describes, with one main verb: controlled. The others lose the main clause, attach the participle to the dresser, or splice with commas.

markScheme.description: The box, which she had packed herself, sat on the dresser

options: The box which she had packed herself and it sat on the dresser
Packing the box herself, the dresser was where it sat
The box she had packed it herself, it sat on the dresser
The box, which she had packed herself, sat on the dresser

questions.prompt: Put the five-minute check in the order the lesson gives it.
questions.solution: Demarcation first because it is the first bullet and the commonest error; speech next because that is where a story goes wrong; then apostrophes, then the hard words, then the ending, because the ending is where content is marked.

items: The ends of sentences: a finger on every full stop
The speech: new lines, punctuation inside, commas after said
Every apostrophe: possession or omission, its and it's
The five most ambitious words, letter by letter

questions.prompt: Correct the non-standard form in: She would of stayed if you had asked.
questions.solution: Would have. The spoken contraction would've sounds like would of, and the of is an error in Standard English. The same applies to should of and could of.

markScheme.description: would have

accepted: she would have stayed if you had asked

questions.prompt: Which of these earns credit as a sentence form for effect?
questions.solution: For effect means placed to do something. The one-word sentence at the turn stops the reader where the story stops. Repetition by accident, an unbroken run-on, and uniform lengths are the opposite of a range.

markScheme.description: A one-word sentence after a long one, at the turn of a story: She looked at the box, at me, at the tea going cold between us. Gone.

options: A one-word sentence after a long one, at the turn of a story: She looked at the box, at me, at the tea going cold between us. Gone.
Every sentence in the piece being exactly the same length, which shows discipline
Every sentence in a paragraph beginning with the same word, so that the reader notices the repetition
A paragraph made of one sentence eleven lines long, so that the reader has to read it twice to follow it, which shows the writer can control a complex structure

questions.prompt: A student writes a compelling story with four comma splices, speech punctuated without commas, and three misspelt ambitious words. Which levels are likely?
questions.solution: The scales are separate. AO5 can be high while AO6 sits where the demarcation and spelling put it: mostly secure and sometimes accurate is the Level 2 wording, and generally accurate spelling is Level 3. Five minutes of checking would have moved the second scale, not the first.

markScheme.description: Level 4 for content and organisation, but Level 2 or 3 for technical accuracy, because demarcation is only sometimes accurate and spelling of ambitious words is not

options: Level 4 on both scales, because the examiners mark the two scales together and a compelling piece carries its accuracy with it, so the errors are overlooked in a strong story
Level 4 for content and organisation, but Level 2 or 3 for technical accuracy, because demarcation is only sometimes accurate and spelling of ambitious words is not
Level 1 on both scales, because errors in punctuation disqualify the content from being credited
Level 4 for technical accuracy, because the story is compelling, and Level 2 for content, because of the errors

questions.prompt: Why does reading the piece backwards, last sentence first, find errors that reading forwards misses?
questions.solution: The flow of sense hides errors: the reader supplies the missing comma and the right spelling from expectation. Sentence by sentence from the end, there is no flow to supply anything, and the splice and the misspelling are visible.

markScheme.description: Because reading forwards the eye predicts the next word and sees what it expects, while reading backwards it must look at each sentence on its own

options: Because errors are more common at the end of a piece, where the writer was tired and hurried, so starting there finds the most errors in the least time
Because the examiners read the piece backwards, and the writer should see what they see
Because reading forwards the eye predicts the next word and sees what it expects, while reading backwards it must look at each sentence on its own
Because backwards reading takes longer, and more time always means more errors found

questions.prompt: Complete the Level 4 descriptor: Uses a full range of appropriate sentence forms for ...
questions.solution: For effect. The phrase is what separates a range from a checklist: the forms are credited when they are placed to do something the reader can feel, the short sentence at the turn, the long one where the mind runs.

markScheme.description: effect

questions.prompt: Put these four punctuation marks in order from the one that joins two sentences to the one that trails off.
questions.solution: Semicolon, colon, dash, ellipsis: from the mark that joins, through the one that introduces and the one that interrupts, to the one that lets the sentence go. Each has one job, and the range the descriptor wants is these used with accuracy, not all of them used often.

markScheme.description: the four marks in order

items: The semicolon, which joins two complete sentences that belong together
The colon, which introduces a list, an explanation or a reveal
The dash, which interrupts a sentence or adds an afterthought
The ellipsis, which trails off and is used once

questions.prompt: Correct every error in this paragraph and then list the errors by class: The house was quiet, everyone had gone to bed accept me. "Are you still up" my mother called from the landing "its nearly midnight". I said I was finishing something, which was true, I was finishing the argument I had lost at dinner, in my head, were I always won. Each of us who had been at the table were asleep by now, there dishes still in the sink.
questions.solution:
Corrected: The house was quiet; everyone had gone to bed except me. "Are you still up?" my mother called from the landing. "It's nearly midnight." I said I was finishing something, which was true: I was finishing the argument I had lost at dinner, in my head, where I always won. Each of us who had been at the table was asleep by now, their dishes still in the sink.

By class. Demarcation: the comma after *quiet* spliced two sentences, replaced by a semicolon; the comma after *true* joined an explanation to its statement, replaced by a colon; the comma after *by now* is kept because what follows is not a sentence. Speech punctuation: the question mark belongs inside the closing mark after *up*; the second speech begins a new sentence, so a full stop after *landing*, a capital *It's* and the full stop inside the final mark. Homophones: *accept* for *except*; *were* for *where*; *there* for *their*. Apostrophe: *its* for *it's*, it is. Agreement: *each of us … were* takes *was*, because the subject is each.

questions.prompt: Write a paragraph of about 150 words describing a kitchen at night, in which you use, correctly and for effect, a semicolon, a colon, a pair of dashes, one line of speech, a one-word sentence, and at least three ambitious words spelt correctly. Then check it in the order the lesson gives.
questions.solution: The kitchen kept its own hours. By day it belonged to everyone; by night it belonged to the tap, which dripped with the patience of something that had never once been in a hurry. There were three things on the table: a mug with a cold half-inch in it, a letter nobody had opened, and the keys. The fridge—an old one, inherited with the house—shuddered every few minutes as if remembering something, and the light it threw when I opened it was the only light I wanted. "You'll wake the whole street," my grandmother said from the doorway, though she said it quietly, and though there was nobody in the street to wake. I closed the door. Dark. She sat down opposite the letter and did not touch it, and the tap went on counting, indifferent, meticulous, and the keys lay between us where they had been all evening.

questions.prompt: A narrator writes: Me and him never did nothing wrong, and it is not inside speech marks. How does the examiner read it?
questions.solution: Outside speech marks the default is Standard English: subject pronouns, one negative. A narrator who speaks in dialect throughout, consistently and by design, is a choice the examiner can see; one non-standard sentence in a standard narration is a lapse of control.

markScheme.description: As non-standard English in the narration, which costs on the Standard English bullet unless the whole narration is in a chosen, consistent voice

options: As a chosen sentence form for effect, which earns credit on the sentence forms bullet because the narrator sounds like a real person rather than a textbook
As correct, because narrators are allowed to speak as they like in a story
As a spelling error, since nothing should be spelt anything

questions.prompt: A student says: 'The examiners care about ideas, not commas.' What is the better account?
questions.solution: AO6 is a fifth of the whole GCSE and it is marked apart from AO5. A compelling piece with splices sits at Level 4 on one scale and Level 2 or 3 on the other, and the difference is five minutes with a finger on every full stop.

markScheme.description: Sixteen of the forty marks on each writing question are for accuracy, marked on a separate scale that ideas cannot rescue, and the five-minute check is the cheapest way to earn marks on the paper

options: Sixteen of the forty marks on each writing question are for accuracy, marked on a separate scale that ideas cannot rescue, and the five-minute check is the cheapest way to earn marks on the paper
The student is right: the AO5 mark is larger, so accuracy hardly matters and the checking time is better spent writing more
The examiners care only about commas, and the ideas are marked by a different examiner who never sees the punctuation or the spelling of the piece at all
The examiners care about ideas on Paper 1 and commas on Paper 2, so accuracy only matters on the second paper

examTechnique.body:
**Sixteen marks on each Question 5, a fifth of the GCSE, marked on its own scale.** Content cannot rescue it, and it is the easier scale to move.

**Keep five minutes, both papers.** Ends of sentences first: a finger on every full stop, and no comma holding two sentences. Then the speech: new lines, punctuation inside, a comma after said. Then every apostrophe. Then the five hardest words, letter by letter. Then the ending.

**Range with a job.** A semicolon that joins, a colon that introduces, a dash that interrupts, used correctly and once or twice, is the wide range the descriptor wants.

**Forms for effect.** The short sentence placed; the long one where the mind runs. A checklist of forms earns nothing.

**Standard English in the narration.** Dialect only inside speech marks, as a choice. Would have, not would of.

**A plain word beats a misspelt ambitious one.**
examinerErrors: Comma splices, which cost the demarcation bullet at every level.
Speech punctuated without commas or with the punctuation outside the closing mark.
Its and it's, whose and who's, their and there, exchanged.
Ambitious words misspelt, especially doubled consonants and -ly endings, which cost on two bullets at once.
Non-standard forms in the narration: would of, me and him, double negatives.
No time kept to check, so that a Level 4 piece for content sits at Level 2 or 3 for accuracy.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 piece is demarcated everywhere: every sentence begins and ends, no comma holds two together, and the only fragments are chosen. Its punctuation has range and a job for each mark, the semicolon joining, the colon introducing, the dashes bracketing, and its speech is set out and punctuated without a slip. Its sentence forms are varied for effect, with the short one placed and the long one running where the mind runs. The narration is Standard English with complex structures under control, and the vocabulary is ambitious because it is exact, and spelt, because five minutes were kept at the end and the check was made in order.
